liturgical_day: Tuesday of the Seventeenth Week in Ordinary Time
epigraph: A nation confesses it has nothing left but the name of God to appeal to.
reflection:
There is a particular kind of prayer that comes only after everything else has failed — not a polished petition, but a cry from the rubble. Jeremiah's voice in the first reading and the disciples' quiet question in the Gospel have almost nothing to do with each other on the surface, and it is worth being honest about that. These two are running on separate tracks today. But each, in its own way, is asking for the same thing: to understand what God is doing in a world that looks, from where we stand, like a wreck.

**The first reading — Jeremiah 14:17-22**

This passage comes from a stretch of Jeremiah sometimes called the "drought liturgy" — a sequence of laments, divine responses, and communal prayers organized around a devastating drought and military catastrophe that fell on Judah in the final decades before the Babylonian exile. By chapter fourteen, the prophet has already heard God refuse to be moved by sacrifices and prayers offered insincerely. What we get here is almost unbearable: Jeremiah is told to weep without rest. He goes out to the fields and sees the dead. He goes into the city and sees the starving. Even the priests and prophets — the people who were supposed to have access to God — are wandering in a land they no longer recognize.

The poem turns, about halfway through, from description to confession. "We recognize, O Lord, our wickedness, the guilt of our fathers; that we have sinned against you." This is significant because throughout the book of Jeremiah, the people have been slow to admit anything. They have been blaming the drought on the wrong gods, turning to foreign alliances, telling themselves that the Temple's presence in Jerusalem guaranteed their safety regardless of how they lived. The confession here is real, and it is desperate.

Then comes what is, for my money, one of the strangest and most moving arguments in all of scripture. The people essentially say to God: among all the idols of the nations, not one of them can produce rain. The heavens themselves cannot send showers on their own. You alone have done all these things — which means you alone can undo them. They are not appealing to their own goodness, because they have just admitted they have none. They are appealing to God's name — to the fact that God is who God is, and that a God who abandons his people entirely would be a different God than the one who made the covenant. It is an argument built entirely from rubble, and it is oddly persuasive.

Psalm 79 is the perfect answer to this reading, because it is not an answer — it is a continuation. It carries the same confession, the same appeal to God's name rather than to human merit, and the same raw honesty about how low things have gotten. "For the glory of your name, O Lord, deliver us." When the congregation sings this refrain back, they are praying with Jeremiah, which is exactly what the liturgy intends.

**The Gospel — Matthew 13:36-43**

The disciples have just heard the parable of the wheat and the weeds — the story of a farmer whose good crop is infiltrated by a weed (almost certainly darnel, a plant that looks exactly like wheat in its early stages and whose roots are so intertwined with wheat that you cannot pull it up without taking the wheat too). The disciples are not satisfied with the story; they want the key. So Jesus goes inside, they follow him, and he gives them the decoded version, term by term.

The explanation is more alarming than the parable. The weeds are real, the enemy who sows them is real, and the final reckoning is real — a fiery furnace, wailing and grinding of teeth. Jesus does not soften this. He is not being cruel; he is being honest with people who are about to go out into a world that will resist everything they preach. But the last image is not fire. It is light: "the righteous will shine like the sun in the Kingdom of their Father." That line deserves to sit for a moment. Not that they will be rewarded, not that they will be safe — that they will *shine*. The image is startling and beautiful, a kind of transfiguration of ordinary faithful life.

Notice also what Jesus does *not* say. He does not tell the disciples to start identifying the weeds. That work belongs to the angels, at the end of the age. The implication is that our job is not sorting — it is growing.

**What patience costs**

If there is a thread between these two readings, it is the cost of waiting. Jeremiah's community is waiting for peace that doesn't come and healing that is replaced by terror. The disciples are asking, implicitly, why the weeds are still there. Both are sitting in conditions that look like abandonment.

The answer the liturgy offers — not loudly, but steadily — is that God's timing is not negligence. Jeremiah's people are held to confession and to the covenant. The disciples are held to trust in a final justice that is not theirs to administer. Both are asked to continue in conditions of uncertainty, which is exactly what faith looks like most days.

**To carry today**

Think about some situation in your life where you are waiting for God to act — a relationship that hasn't healed, a prayer that seems to go nowhere, some injustice that keeps standing. Ask yourself honestly: am I still willing to appeal to God's name, even when I have nothing else to offer? Notice whether your prayer today can be honest enough to sound like Jeremiah's.

liturgical_day: Monday of the Seventeenth Week in Ordinary Time
epigraph: A rotted loincloth and a mustard seed: God works in the concrete and the small.
reflection:
Today's readings are, on the surface, doing two very different things. Jeremiah is staging a grim object lesson about a nation that has drifted away from God, while Matthew's Jesus is sketching the Kingdom in quick, almost playful images. These two are largely on separate tracks — the prophet's grief and the parables' quiet confidence belong to different moments in salvation history. But there is a thread worth noticing, not forced but real: God keeps working through the ordinary and the material, through cloth and seeds and flour, refusing to stay abstract.

**The first reading — Jeremiah 13:1-11**

We are early in the book of Jeremiah, in the section scholars call his "symbolic actions" — moments when the prophet is asked to *do* something strange in public, or in private, as a kind of living parable. He has already smashed a clay pot at the city gate. Now he is told to buy a linen loincloth, wear it for a time without washing it, then walk to the Parath and bury it in a rock cleft. He waits. He goes back. He digs it up. It is ruined, rotted through, completely useless.

The word translated "loincloth" here is important: this is not a belt or a sash but an undergarment, the piece of clothing worn closest to the body. When God says that Israel and Judah were meant to cling to him the way this garment clings to a man's body, the image is intimate to the point of being almost startling. This is not the language of alliance or covenant obligation in its legal sense — it is the language of closeness, of belonging, of being bound to another by habit and proximity and daily life. They were supposed to be his *people, his renown, his praise, his beauty.* Those are words of pride, even of delight.

And then they did not listen. The loincloth, buried in the earth and left there through neglect, rots. It becomes good for nothing. That, says God through Jeremiah, is what has happened to the people who were meant to wear his name.

The responsorial psalm is drawn from the Song of Moses in Deuteronomy — one of the oldest poems in the Hebrew Bible — and it answers Jeremiah with almost the same ache. "You were unmindful of the Rock that begot you, you forgot the God who gave you birth." The word "forgot" is doing heavy lifting there. This is not the forgetting of ignorance; it is the forgetting that comes from distraction, from slowly looking elsewhere until the original face has gone dim.

There is something almost darkly comic about God's response in the psalm — "I will provoke them with a 'no-people'; with a foolish nation I will anger them." God will use their own method against them: they have given their devotion to a "no-god," to idols that are hollow, and so he will stir their jealousy through a people they would not bother to notice. Even the divine grief has a kind of exasperated wit to it.

**The Gospel — Matthew 13:31-35**

Matthew 13 is the great parable chapter, and we have been moving through it for several days now. Jesus has already explained the sower and the wheat and the weeds. Now he offers two shorter parables, each barely a sentence long, and each turning on something almost laughably small becoming inexplicably large.

The mustard seed was proverbial in Jewish teaching as the smallest measurable thing — so small it was nearly invisible when held in the palm. Yet in the right conditions it grows into a plant large enough for birds to nest in. The yeast parable works the same way from the opposite direction: a woman folds a small amount of leaven into a large amount of flour — three measures is closer to fifty pounds than to a dinner quantity — and it works through the whole batch invisibly, from within.

Matthew tells us that Jesus spoke only in parables to the crowds, and he ties this to Psalm 78: "I will open my mouth in parables, I will announce what has lain hidden from the foundation of the world." There is something Jesus wants to say about the Kingdom that cannot be said directly, only shown sideways, through images that do their work slowly, the way yeast does.

**Where smallness is the point**

The connection worth sitting with today is this: both readings take God's activity seriously in the particular and the physical. Jeremiah is not given a vision or a dream; he is told to walk to the market, buy cloth, wear it, and get his hands dirty in a rock cleft beside the river. Jesus does not describe the Kingdom as a theological category; he points to a seed and a woman at work in her kitchen.

The loincloth and the mustard seed are not decorations hung on an idea. They are the idea. God works in the material world, through the concrete, the daily, the embarrassingly small. The tragedy in Jeremiah is that Israel looked past the tangible gifts — the land, the law, the daily provision — toward the spectacle of the idols. The hope in Matthew is that the Kingdom is already at work in what looks like nothing, doing what yeast does: changing everything from inside.

**To carry today**

Consider where in your own life you are waiting for the large and obvious sign while something small has already been placed in front of you — a returning habit of prayer, a small act of patience, an almost-invisible change in how you treat someone. Ask whether you have the patience to let the hidden thing do its quiet work.

epigraph: Solomon asks for one thing; the merchant sells everything — both know what is worth wanting.
reflection:
There is a particular kind of clarity that comes over a person when they finally know what they want. Not what they want to want, not what they think they should want — but the thing itself, seen plain, and recognized as worth any cost. Today's readings circle this experience from different angles, and together they raise a question worth sitting with all week: do I actually know what I am looking for?

**The first reading — 1 Kings 3:5, 7-12**

This passage arrives early in the reign of Solomon, David's son, and the scene is a dream. God appears and offers Solomon anything — which is the kind of sentence that stops you cold when you read it slowly. *Anything.* The offer is real; this is not a riddle or a test of nerve. It is a blank check extended to a new king who has just inherited the most powerful throne in the region and who, by his own admission, is young, uncertain, and overwhelmed.

What follows is one of the most quietly remarkable moments in the Hebrew scriptures. Solomon does not ask for long life, or wealth, or victory over his enemies — the three things a sensible advisor would have told him to want. Instead he asks for an understanding heart. The Hebrew behind that phrase suggests something closer to a *listening* heart, a heart that can hear what a situation truly requires, not just what it appears to require on the surface. He wants to be able to tell right from wrong in the complex, tangled, human business of governing real people with real grievances.

God's pleasure at this response is explicit and almost touching. Because Solomon did not ask for the things he could reasonably have wanted — and which God would presumably have granted — he receives something rarer. A wisdom so deep that, the text says, no one before him had it and no one after him will equal it.

Psalm 119 answers this directly. It is the great long psalm of love for God's law, and the verses chosen today strike exactly the same note: the psalmist prizes God's commands above silver and gold. Not as a pious sentiment, but as a tested judgment — the law gives light, gives direction, gives life. The psalm and the first reading together are making a claim: that wisdom, properly understood, is not a human achievement but a gift that flows from loving what God loves.

**The second reading — Romans 8:28-30**

Paul's letter to the Romans is moving, in these middle chapters, through a dense and beautiful argument about what God has been doing in human history — and in individual human lives — from the very beginning. These three verses are among the most consoling in the entire New Testament, and they are also, if you look at them straight, among the most dizzying. Paul strings together a chain of verbs — foreknew, predestined, called, justified, glorified — and each one carries the weight of a whole theology. He is not promising that good things will happen to people who love God; he is saying that the whole sweep of a life, including its hard and confusing stretches, is held inside a purpose larger than any single moment can reveal.

This reading is on its own track today, in the sense that it does not tie neatly into the images of the kingdom from Solomon and Matthew. But it sets a frame around them. If God's call and purpose are as comprehensive as Paul says, then the longing Solomon feels for wisdom, and the longing the merchant feels for the pearl, are not random. They are part of something being worked out from a direction we cannot fully see.

**The Gospel — Matthew 13:44-52**

This is the third and final Sunday in Matthew's great parable chapter, and Jesus offers three parables here in quick succession. The treasure hidden in a field, the pearl of great price, and the net — and then a small coda about the scribe who is like a householder drawing from a storeroom both old things and new.

The treasure and the pearl are often read as a pair, and they are, but they have a subtle difference that is worth noticing. The man who finds the treasure stumbles on it — he was not searching for it specifically; it was just there, in a field he happened to be working. The merchant, on the other hand, is a professional seeker. He has been looking for fine pearls his whole career. One man finds by accident; the other finds by long, intentional search. But the response is identical: both sell *everything* they have, and do so with what the text quietly calls joy. This is not anguish or sacrifice in the tragic sense. It is the relief of a person who has finally found the thing that makes all other things make sense, and who parts with them not grudgingly but gladly.

The net parable that follows is darker — it acknowledges that not everything hauled in is worth keeping, and that a sorting will come. Jesus is not letting his disciples off the hook entirely. But notice that he ends not with the sorting but with the scribe and the storeroom: the one who has learned the kingdom draws on everything, old wisdom and new revelation alike, and finds use for all of it.

**What wisdom costs — and what it frees**

Solomon gives up the easier asks. The merchant gives up his inventory. What both gain in return is not a thing they can hoard but a capacity — to see rightly, to judge rightly, to know what matters. That is the connection the readings are making: real wisdom is recognizable by what it makes a person willing to release. The man who clutches his gold and his silver and his long life at the expense of understanding has not made a wise trade. He has made the trade of someone who does not yet know what the field contains.

**To carry today**

Think about what you are actually asking for when you pray — what you hope for, what you would choose if the choice were laid bare. Are those the things that would make you more capable of love, more able to see what is right, more free? That is not a rebuke; it is an honest question worth bringing to the quiet of the day.

epigraph: A mother asks for thrones; Jesus offers a cup — and James drinks it.
reflection:
James, the son of Zebedee, was martyred by Herod Agrippa around the year 44, making him the first of the Twelve to die for the faith. He left behind no letter, no Gospel, no recorded sermon. What we have instead is a story about his mother asking for the wrong thing on his behalf, and the quiet fact that when the cup came around, he drank it. The Church keeps his feast in red, the color of blood, and the readings she gives him are not comfortable ones.

**The first reading — 2 Corinthians 4:7-15**

Paul is writing to a community that has started to doubt him. His opponents have apparently argued that a genuine apostle wouldn't look so battered — wouldn't be so often imprisoned, hungry, shipwrecked, or afraid. Real authority, they suggest, would be more impressive. Paul's response is one of the most quietly stunning passages in all his letters: yes, exactly, that is precisely the point. The treasure — meaning the gospel, the knowledge of God revealed in Christ — is being carried in earthen vessels, which is the Greek way of saying clay pots. Ordinary, breakable, worth almost nothing in themselves.

The image would have landed hard for Paul's original readers, because clay jars were everywhere in the ancient world and they were understood to be temporary containers. You did not treasure a clay jar; you treasured what was inside it. Paul is saying that the apostle himself is the clay jar. His weakness, his suffering, his very un-glamorous appearance is not evidence against his mission but evidence of where the power actually comes from.

What follows is a string of paradoxes so carefully balanced they feel almost like a creed: afflicted but not constrained, perplexed but not despairing, struck down but not destroyed. Each pair holds the weight without resolving it — Paul is not saying the suffering doesn't hurt, he is saying it doesn't have the last word. And the reason is specific: he is "always carrying about in the body the dying of Jesus." This is not metaphor for Paul; it is a literal description of what apostolic life has cost him. The death is real. But so is the logic that follows — if the dying of Jesus is present in the body, then the life of Jesus may also be manifested there.

Psalm 126 sits alongside this with its image of those who go out weeping, carrying seed, and come back carrying sheaves. The psalm was originally about the return from exile in Babylon — the shock of captives discovering, almost disbelieving, that they were going home. Paul is living inside exactly that movement: the exile of suffering, the homecoming of resurrection.

**The Gospel — Matthew 20:20-28**

There is something genuinely touching about the mother of James and John marching up to Jesus and asking for the best seats in the Kingdom. Matthew gives us the mother as the speaker; Mark has the brothers ask directly themselves. Either way, the request is the same and the embarrassment is the same — she wants her boys on the right and left of Jesus when he comes into his glory.

Jesus doesn't mock her for it. He turns and speaks to the sons: "Can you drink the chalice that I am going to drink?" And they say, without hesitation, that they can. They almost certainly have no idea what they are agreeing to. They are thinking about glory; he is thinking about Gethsemane. But here is what the Church holds onto on this feast day: they said yes, and eventually they meant it. James would be beheaded. The cup would come, and he would drink it — not because he was fearless, but because he had said yes to something larger than he understood.

Jesus then gathers all twelve and explains what authority is going to look like among them. The Gentile rulers lord it over their subjects; greatness among the disciples is to work the other way entirely — the greatest is the servant, the first is the slave. And then the sentence that grounds all of it: the Son of Man did not come to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many. He is not issuing a rule about church governance in the abstract. He is describing himself, and he is saying: be like this.

**Ambition turned inside out**

What holds these readings together is the question of what power is actually for. The mother wants her sons elevated; Paul is writing from a posture of radical diminishment; James ends up executed. The trajectory of the Gospel is not upward mobility but downward service — and not because suffering is good in itself, but because something gets through in the broken places that cannot get through any other way. Paul's clay jar carries the treasure precisely because the jar doesn't get in the way. James's death bore witness to something no living comfortable apostle could have said quite so clearly.

This is not a comfortable feast. But it is an honest one, and there is something freeing about the honesty. The Church is not asking us to be more impressive. She is asking us to be more available — to what is being poured in, and to where it needs to go.

**To carry today**

Think of something you are carrying right now that feels like pure loss — a situation that has cost you something and shows no sign of producing anything. Ask whether it might, despite appearances, be one of those places where something is getting through that couldn't get through any other way. You don't have to feel that yet. Just stay open to the possibility that the jar being broken is not the end of the story.

liturgical_day: Friday of the Sixteenth Week in Ordinary Time
epigraph: God gathers the scattered; the question is what kind of soil we give him to work with.
reflection:
Two passages, one from the prophet and one from the Lord himself, and they are not quite on the same track — Jeremiah is speaking of exile and return, and Jesus is explaining a parable about hearing. But they rhyme in a way that is worth noticing: both are about what happens when the word of God actually lands somewhere, and both are quietly urgent about it.

**The first reading — Jeremiah 3:14-17**

By the time we reach chapter three of Jeremiah, the prophet has already laid out the charge against Israel at some length. The people have been unfaithful — not in some vague spiritual sense, but in the specific, political, religious chaos of the late seventh century before Christ, when the nation was hemorrhaging its allegiance to God and patching it back together with idols and foreign alliances. The tone of the opening chapters is by turns indignant and heartbroken, and what makes Jeremiah remarkable is that the heartbreak belongs not just to the prophet but to God himself. The LORD speaks in this book the way a husband speaks of a wife who has left — not coldly, not with bureaucratic judgment, but with a grief that keeps reasserting itself even in the accusation.

So when verse 14 opens with "Return, rebellious children," the word "rebellious" in the original carries something like the idea of turning away, of an about-face in the wrong direction. And yet the sentence doesn't end in punishment — it ends in gathering. "I will take you, one from a city, two from a clan, and bring you to Zion." That image is worth sitting with: not a mass return, not a parade, but a patient individual rescue — one person here, two families there — as though God is going house to house. The numbers suggest a remnant, a small and scattered group, not a triumphant national restoration. But the tenderness is in the detail.

Then comes something startling. The LORD says that in those coming days, people will no longer speak of the ark of the covenant, no longer miss it or look for it or try to rebuild it. For Israel, the ark was the most sacred object in existence — the gold-covered chest housing the tablets of the law, the physical sign of God's presence with the people. Its loss to the Babylonians was catastrophic. And yet here God says: don't worry about the ark. Jerusalem itself will be called the LORD's throne. The presence of God will not be contained in an object; it will fill the city, and through the city, draw all nations. It is a promise so large it is almost hard to absorb — an end to the exile of the heart, not just the exile from the land.

The psalm, drawn from Jeremiah 31 rather than from Psalms, sings this same hope back in a warmer register: the scattered are gathered, mourning turns to joy, the young and the old dance together. It is the same promise sung rather than declared.

**The Gospel — Matthew 13:18-23**

This is not the parable of the sower itself — that came the day before, and the disciples asked Jesus what it meant. This is Jesus answering. It is a rare thing in the Gospels: an explicit, point-by-point interpretation given by Jesus himself. Usually he leaves the parables open, lets them work in the listener. Here he closes the loop, probably because the disciples have asked directly and because he trusts them with more than the crowd receives.

The fourfold soil — the hard path, the rocky ground, the thorny patch, the good earth — maps onto four kinds of hearing. What is striking is that three of the four actually receive the word. The seed falls. The problem in most cases is not that the word is absent but that something prevents it from taking root: incomprehension in the first case, shallow enthusiasm without depth in the second, the slow suffocation of anxiety and wealth in the third. Only the last hearer both receives and understands — and the verb "understands" here is doing real work. It doesn't mean intellectual mastery; it means something closer to taking in, absorbing, letting the word become part of how you see and act.

The yields — a hundred, sixty, thirtyfold — are agricultural extravagances. A Palestinian farmer would have been delighted with a tenfold return. Jesus is describing not merely adequate fruit but abundance.

**Hearing as homecoming**

What connects Jeremiah and Matthew today is not a shared image but a shared question: what does it take for the word of God to actually arrive? Jeremiah's God is gathering a scattered people one by one — it is an act of pure initiative, God doing the seeking. Jesus describes the word going out like seed, falling on every kind of ground — that too is God's initiative, prodigal and unprejudiced. But in both cases, something is required on the receiving end. The scattered have to be willing to return; the soil has to be what it is.

Jeremiah promises that God will appoint shepherds "after my own heart" to tend the gathered people wisely. The psalm echoes it: the Lord himself is the shepherd who guards the flock. And in Matthew, the word that the good-soil hearer receives and understands is precisely the word of the Kingdom — the news that the shepherd is here, that the gathering has begun, that even now the seed is going out.

The invitation is not to anxiety about which soil we are. It is to notice whether we are actually hearing.

**To carry today**

Think about where your attention goes when you sit with something difficult — a scripture reading, a conversation you didn't want to have, a question about your own life. Do you absorb it, or does something else quickly crowd it out? Ask today for one moment of genuine attention, of letting something you hear actually land and stay.

liturgical_day: Thursday of the Sixteenth Week in Ordinary Time
epigraph: God remembers the love of the beginning, and keeps offering the living water we keep refusing.
reflection:
There is a marriage gone wrong at the heart of today's first reading, and a crowd that cannot quite see what is standing right in front of them in the Gospel. Both are stories about a strange and persistent blindness — the kind that is not accidental but chosen, not a failure of information but a failure of desire. What makes these readings worth sitting with is that neither God nor Jesus gives up because of it.

**The first reading — Jeremiah 2:1-3, 7-8, 12-13**

Jeremiah is one of the great tragic figures of the Hebrew scriptures. He prophesied for decades in Jerusalem before its fall to Babylon in 587 B.C., watching the city ignore warning after warning. What we have today is almost the opening of his public ministry — a kind of prosecution speech delivered on God's behalf to the city. It is worth knowing that the speech is not angry in the way we might expect. It opens with something closer to grief.

God recalls the early days of Israel's relationship with him — the desert years, the wilderness wandering after the Exodus. That period was not, historically, a golden age in any simple sense; the wilderness stories are full of complaint and rebellion. But the image here reaches past the historical record toward something true in another register: there was a time of nearness, of dependence, of being carried. "I remember the devotion of your youth," God says, "how you loved me as a bride." The marriage metaphor would have been startling when Jeremiah first spoke it, and it remains startling. The God of the universe is describing himself as a husband who remembers when his wife first loved him.

Then the indictment. God brought Israel into "the garden land," the promised territory, and what happened next was a betrayal on every level of society: priests who stopped asking where God was, scribes and lawyers who knew the law but had forgotten its author, shepherds — this is the word for leaders, kings and elders — who outright rebelled, and prophets who were prophesying in the name of Baal, the Canaanite storm-deity whose worship was everywhere in the culture around them. Every layer of leadership had failed.

The image that closes the passage is one of the most arresting in all of Jeremiah. God calls on the heavens themselves to be horrified at what has happened, and then delivers the double charge: Israel has abandoned "the source of living waters" and instead dug cisterns — holding tanks carved out of limestone — that are broken and cannot hold water. It is almost darkly comic if you think about it too long. Cisterns were genuinely useful things, but they held only rainwater, stagnant and still, and this image is of ones that are cracked besides. Someone has walked away from a running spring to lug water in a leaking bucket. The sheer foolishness of it is part of the point.

Psalm 36 answers this reading with precise and beautiful irony. "With you is the fountain of life, O Lord" — the very thing Jeremiah accuses Israel of abandoning. The psalm does not argue or explain; it simply sets the reality back in front of us: the mercy reaches to heaven, the stream is delightful, the light is yours when you stand in God's light.

**The Gospel — Matthew 13:10-17**

Matthew 13 is the great parable chapter, and what we get today is not a parable itself but a conversation about why Jesus uses them. The disciples ask a reasonable question: why not just say plainly what you mean? The crowds are right there.

Jesus's answer has troubled readers for a long time, because it sounds almost cruel at first hearing — as if he is deliberately obscuring the truth from people so they cannot be converted. But the logic is more precise than that. He is quoting Isaiah 6, the prophet's own call narrative, in which Isaiah is sent to a people whose hearts have already closed themselves. Jesus is observing the same pattern, not engineering it. The parables are not a mechanism of exclusion; they are a form of truth-telling that can only be received by those who are willing to receive it. A story about seeds and soil lands differently depending on what kind of soil you are.

The word for "gross" in the Isaiah quotation — "gross is the heart of this people" — carries the sense of grown thick, calloused, like skin that has been rubbed so long it no longer feels. It is not a permanent condition; conversion is still explicitly named as what would happen if they would only see and hear. The door is not locked from the outside.

**The blindness that is a choice**

What Jeremiah and Matthew share is the portrait of a specifically chosen blindness. Israel in Jeremiah does not lack information; she has the law, the prophets, the priests, the memory of the Exodus. The crowds around Jesus do not lack access; they are standing in front of him. What is missing in both cases is the willingness to let what they see actually land, to let it cost them the comfortable explanations they have already arranged. That is the harder diagnosis, because it applies well past ancient Israel and first-century Galilee.

The good news in both readings is the same: the living water is still flowing, the door is still open, and the disciples — ordinary, confused, often stumbling — are told that their eyes are *blessed* because they see.

**To carry today**

Consider where in your life you might already have your explanation settled before you look. The broken cisterns in Jeremiah are not wicked things — they are just our own anxious arrangements, the strategies we trust because we made them ourselves. Ask today for the grace to look at one situation in your life with a little less certainty about what you will find, and a little more willingness to be surprised by what is actually there.

epigraph: Looking for a body, she hears her name, and everything changes.
reflection:
**The first reading — Song of Songs 3:1-4b**

The Song of Songs is the strangest book in the Bible to find at Mass. It is a love poem, erotic and restless, set in the streets of a city at night. The bride gets up from her bed and goes looking — through the streets, past the watchmen, past anyone who might help — and finds the one she loves almost by accident, almost before she can say where she found him. The poem ends in the middle of the embrace.

The Church has long read this book as something more than a wedding song: the soul in search of God, desire as a form of theology. That reading doesn't erase the poem's plainness — the woman really is looking, really is desperate, really does find — but it gives the searching a shape that fits today's feast exactly. Mary Magdalene at the tomb is the bride in the streets, except her beloved is not missing. He is present. She cannot recognize him.

**The Gospel — John 20:1-2, 11-18**

John's account of Easter morning is built around a misrecognition. Mary sees the risen Christ and thinks she is looking at the gardener. She is so fixed on finding the body she came to anoint that she cannot read what is standing in front of her. And then he says her name — one word, *Mary* — and everything reorganizes itself. She does not recognize the risen Christ by sight. She recognizes him by the way he says her name.

What happens next is often overlooked. He tells her not to hold on to him, and then sends her — *go and tell my brothers*. She came to tend a corpse and leaves as a witness to a resurrection. She is the first to carry the news of Easter, which is why she has been called, in a title the tradition takes seriously, the apostle to the apostles.

**What the two readings share**

The psalm holds both readings together: *my soul is thirsting for you, my flesh pines for you, like the earth parched and without water.* That thirst runs through the Song's bride in the streets and through Mary bent weeping into an empty tomb. Both are looking in the wrong place for the right person. The moment of finding, in both cases, comes not through their searching but through being known — recognized, named, encountered from the other side.

What the Song cannot give you, John completes: the beloved does not just appear. He speaks.

**To carry today**

What are you so sure you're looking for that you might not recognize it when it's already there?
